## Reference-entry detection, fired on the anthology

*2026-10-01 02:00:04*

**The forcing function had been answered by the bibliography.** The anthology
opted ten fields into `explain: cited`. Asked whether that was making its
prose richer, the measurement said no. About half of the 1427 explained
relations were satisfied by a document's own reference line, `Author (Year),
LIT-nnn — ARXIV-…`, which names the paper and says nothing about it. The
check only bit on the 81 relations whose code appeared nowhere at all.

**The detector reads shape, because the heading is one record's habit.** The
first idea was to skip `## Source`. That fails on every record that names the
section differently, and it would skip annotated entries filed under it.
`luria/bibliography.py` judges each paragraph or list item on its own, by
four signals:
- an author lead that ends at a year, or a classic list of initials and
  surnames;
- identifiers;
- a title, dropped only when a venue or an identifier follows it;
- how much prose is left over.

**What separated entries from prose was case, not connectives.** The first
version asked for two function words among six leftover words. On the
anthology it hid "Two groups, three months apart, the same bug and two
different fixes." and "Two groups, two corpora, two instruments, no citation
in either direction." Both are annotations, terse enough to have almost no
connectives. Counting lower-case words fixed both. Names, initials and
acronyms are capitalised, so authors surviving from a second entry on the
line no longer count as prose either. Now eight lower-case words, or five
with two connectives, read as prose.

**Missed shapes found on the real corpus, each now a test:**
- an affiliation after `et al.` (`Shi et al., Meta (2023)`);
- a lower-case corporate author (`The Movie Gen team (2024)`);
- affiliations containing `of` and `at` (`University of Texas at Austin`);
- `and colleagues`.

The classic formats (APA, numbered, markdown link lists) were never seen on
the anthology, and are in the tests on their own merit.

**Fired on the anthology with the ten fields as configured: 590
findings**, all of them "cites X only in a reference entry (line n)":
- `SOTA.source` 267;
- `SOTA.introduced_by` 253;
- `THEORY.source` 70.

Every other explained field was already discussed in prose. Two checks of
the result:
- **The line-based count disagreed on 133.** Sampled, they are explanations
  that wrap onto the next line, or annotated entries. The block-level
  judgement is right about them.
- **38 of the 590 discuss the paper by its first author's name without the
  code** ("…Hoffmann et al."). That is still a finding worth having: the fix
  is to write the code in that sentence, which the anthology's own linking
  rule asks for anyway.

## A vocabulary is a scheme in shorthand

*2026-10-01 18:30:16*

**The question was hierarchy.** [#298](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/298) proposed union vocabularies, and behind
it sat a bigger ask: can a record express a hierarchical ontology? A sweep of
the code, the decisions, the docs and the issues found nothing. `groups:` is
a single level, a group is not a value anyone can tag with, and nothing rolls
up. A union would have added composition (one field accepting a cat or a
dog) but not subsumption: "cat" would still not be a term.

**The experiment that settled it used records, not config.** A `TERM`
scheme with a `broader`/`narrower` converse, a chain over `broader`, and
notes citing terms through a reference rendered Pet → Cat → {Tabby, Calico}
as a tree. It refused a citation of a term that did not exist, and gave
every term a status. So the hierarchy was already expressible; what the
record lacked was the move from vocabulary to scheme. The owner's reading:
a vocabulary is a tiny constrained scheme, and a record that wants more from
one is showing a type error, so the mechanism to build is promotion, not a
richer vocabulary ([ADR-124](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-124.md)).

**The trap was the views.** Hand-converting a vocabulary in a scratch
record linted clean and silently lost two things:

- **Index grouping.** The index could group only by a `fields:` entry, and
  `axis` refused a reference. Nothing listed which RFCs were in an area any
  more, except the published site's backlinks.
- **The old pages.** `docs/rfcs/area/runtime.md` was left behind. The
  directory stopped being one the generator owns once the field stopped
  being grouped, so `luria index` neither rewrote nor removed it, and
  nothing reported it.

The first is now `group: true` on a reference (and `axis` may name one), so
promotion keeps its views. Promotion keeps the field grouped, which makes
the second a non-issue for promotion. It remains a gap for any field that
stops being grouped by hand.

A converse listing each term's members was the cheaper alternative, and was
rejected. It needs no index change, but it makes every tagged document edit
its term's file, which turns popular terms into merge hot spots ([DP-2](../../record/principles.d/DP-002.md)).

**Things found on the way:**

- **The migration scaffold was still TOML.** `luria new migration` wrote
  `title = "…"` into a `.yaml` file that `luria migrate` reads with
  `yaml.safe_load`, where it parsed as one string. A test pinned the TOML
  spelling, so the suite had been enforcing the bug. The scaffold is YAML
  now, and a test parses its commented examples into operations the
  planner knows.
- **A dry run swept for nothing.** It walked every tracked file even when
  the plan had no code renames, which also made it need git. It now skips
  the walk unless there is something to sweep.
- **`modeling.md` still pointed at `statuses.yaml`.** Its "smells" section
  named the file — another stale mention of it, found after
  the second review. Grepping for the vocabulary of a stale claim is what
  finds them, and reading the flagged line is not.
- **The decision-shaped template leaked into promoted terms.** With no
  `_template.md`, `new_scheme_doc` falls back to a form that seeds
  `tags: [record]` and "Why this needed deciding" prose. Promotion now
  writes the scheme's template and stub the way `luria init` does, drops
  the seeded `tags`, and uses the value's blurb (or a provenance line) as
  the body.

**Then the numbers.** Promotion first rewrote `area: [runtime]` to
`area: [AREA-001]`: typed, checked, and unreadable. Derived aliases
already existed ([ADR-088](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-088.md)). A scheme's `alias: "AREA-{slug}"` makes
`AREA-runtime` resolve to AREA-001, and the fixer keeps it. But only prose
honoured them: a reference field rejected `AREA-runtime` as "not a code",
and so did `luria relate`. Every reader of a reference value had its own
resolution:
- the contract;
- the typed edges;
- two copies of `_codes` in chains and relations;
- invariants' `held`;
- the grouping;
- `relate`.

They now share one, `aliases.derived_code`. The converse fixer writes the
alias spelling too, and drops either spelling, because a removal by code
alone would have silently missed an alias.

The alias is derived from the slug, not the title. A title is a label: it
has spaces and capitals, and can differ from the value entirely. The slug
*is* the old value, so documents keep reading as they did. An alias tail
allows only letters, digits, dots and hyphens, so `long_term` slugs to
`long-term`. Two values slugging alike, or one that would read as a number
(`AREA-7` is a code, and a code outranks an alias), are refused.

Linting this repository took the same time with alias resolution on the
reference path (5.6s against 5.4s on `main`). The alias map is cached per
config, and the lookup runs only when some scheme declares an alias.

## A fresh record should have nothing to say

*2026-10-02 05:52:56*

**[#331](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/331), and why the existing guard missed it.**
`test_a_fresh_default_init_lints_clean` runs `init`, `index` and `lint`. But
`lint.run()` only raises on violations, so warnings passed it, and three of
them printed on every new record. The new test (`tests/test_fresh_init.py`)
captures what `lint` prints and requires nothing but the all-clear. It covers
the default config and a custom one with no principles scheme, which is the
shape the RFC tutorial uses.

**CLAUDE.md was a copy, not a plan.** `docs/README.md` has been planned from
the config since [ADR-048](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-048.md). `CLAUDE.md` was copied verbatim, and its first
paragraph links `docs/design-principles.md`. In a record with no principles
scheme that link points at a page nothing will ever generate, and
`broken-targets` said so on day one. The paragraph now follows the config.
It points where a document-rendered scheme writes `paths.design_principles`,
and is left out when no scheme does. The broken links seen *before* the
first `luria index` are a different matter: those pages are generated, and
`init` already says to index before linting, so that state is expected.

**`spent-upgrades` was talking to the wrong reader.** Its own devlog entry
(2026-09-06) describes it firing on luria's record "the moment its own
upgrade ran, which is the guard working". The remedy it names, "remove it at
1.0.0", is a change to luria. A downstream record can't make that change. A
record born on YAML never needed the upgrade at all, so for its owner the
row could only teach them to skim past a finding.

Two narrower fixes didn't hold up:
- **Look at git history** for a `luria.toml` the record once had. Both this
  checkout and CI's are shallow, so the answer would depend on clone depth.
- **Have `init` write a `mute` line.** `init` never overwrites a
  `luria.yaml`, so the tutorial path, where the config is written first,
  wouldn't get it.

What does hold is scoping by who can act. The finding is reported only when
the running `luria/upgrade.py` lives inside the record's root, which is true
for luria's own checkout because CI installs it editable (`pip-spec: -e .`).
Along the way: `spent_upgrades()` runs one plan (the statuses one) for every
entry in `SUNSET`, so the `yaml` row has never been checked on its own. That
is unchanged here.

**`collect` crashed on the directory `init` had just made.** The default
`record/changelog.d` has a target, `CHANGELOG.md`, that nothing wrote.
`init` now writes each fragment directory's target with a heading and the
insert marker. `collect` still refuses to create a missing target itself:
what goes above the marker is a choice about the file. But the refusal is
now a message that names the file and says `luria init` writes it, instead
of a `FileNotFoundError`.

## A catch-all keyword swallows --help

*2026-10-02 12:48:14*

**[#328](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/328).** `luria new --help` answered "no such field 'help'". Fire shows a
function's help when it sees `--help` only if the function has no
`**kwargs` to hand it to. `new.run` has one: it accepts a scheme's declared
fields as flags (`--source LIT-134` where SOTA declares `source`). So
`--help` arrived as `declared={'help': True}` and was refused like any
undeclared field. Any other command that grows a catch-all will do the same.

The fix pops `help`/`h` before field parsing, and prints the one thing the
generic Fire help never could: the kinds this record scaffolds and the flags
each takes, read from `luria.yaml` like the dispatch ([ADR-036](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-036.md)). Those are
what a first-time reader gets wrong. The first docs draft wrote
`luria new RFC` four times, when kinds are the lowercased prefix. One
per-kind flag list (`accepted_flags`) now feeds both help and the refusal
message. The refusal had been listing a scheme's declared `status` and
`tags` twice, once as universal flags and once as declared fields.

Not done here: a fragment or journal still accepts flags it ignores
(`luria new changelog --title`, [#330](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/330)). `accepted_flags` is the list a
refusal would read.

## Duplicate keys: ask the parser

*2026-10-02 15:26:26*

**[#240](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/240).** The duplicate-key half of `frontmatter_shape` compared the raw text before the first colon, on unindented lines only. That approximates YAML without being YAML: `"title":` after `title:`, and any repeated key in a nested mapping, both collapsed silently. That is the [#164](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/164) defect again in other spellings. The check now loads the block with a `SafeLoader` subclass that refuses a repeated key in any mapping, so the parser that does the collapsing is the one asked. The `<!--` half stays a text check, because no loader raises on a key that happens to read `<!--`.

Two details the issue's sketch did not cover:
- **`<<` merge keys** are skipped. An explicit key after a merge is how YAML spells an override.
- **The line number** comes free from the key node's mark, so the finding names it. The issue had expected to lose it.

**Journals were never checked.** `check_journals` parsed frontmatter but never called the shape check, so a devlog entry could pass the lint and still fail the Pages build. It now runs the same check, and still reads its metadata through the cached `read_document`.

**Fired once on a real case.** The issue's repro (`"title": dup` above `title:` in [ADR-124](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-124.md)) and a nested duplicate in a real devlog entry were both reported with the right lines, then reverted. This record lints clean under the stricter check. Lint time: 5.8s against 5.4s on `main`, using the C loader where it is built.

## Forbidding a field: the mirror of required_when

*2026-10-02 16:25:50*

**[#191](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/191) was still open after a month of features.** Before building, I checked whether anything since could express it. `excluded_by` (now on any field since [ADR-098](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-098.md)) compares values within one field. `field_groups` counts present fields, and `status` is always present. Derived fields have no conditionals. The issue's exact case still linted clean on `main`. So `forbidden_when` takes `required_when`'s condition in the opposite sense ([ADR-125](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-125.md)). The built-in successor field forbids itself while `status` is the scheme's `active` word.

**One condition, two keys.** `_when` parses the shape for both keys, and `_conditions` yields both to the same load-time check, so a misspelled field or value fails for either. Contradictions are refused at load: required and forbidden, a value in both lists, and forbidden on a field with a `default`. The last is easy to miss. A default is never absent, so the rule would fire on documents that never wrote the field.

**Three existing tests were standing in the forbidden state.** Two contract tests and an annotation test put `superseded_by` on an `Active` fixture, because nothing had ever said that was wrong. They were about remote resolution and the annotation fixer, not status, so their fixtures now retire the document first.

**The annotation fixer refused on its own.** `annotations` already declines a write that would leave a document in breach of its contract. A `ref::superseded_by:` annotation on an `Active` note is now reported as a bad annotation instead of being written. No new code was needed for that, and a test now pins it.

**Fired once on a real case.** In a scratch record from `luria init`, [ADR-001](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-001.md) at `Active` with `superseded_by: [ADR-002]` printed `luria: docs lint clean` on `main`. On this branch it is a violation naming `status: Active` and the ADR. This record and every example lint clean under the rule, so none of them held the contradiction.

**Not mine:** `ADR-122.md:123: ref::extended_by names no reference field` prints on `main` too.

## Title comparison folds spelling, not meaning

*2026-10-02 19:38:00*

**[#340](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/340).** arXiv began returning a title in TeX (`$O(n^2)$`), and `normalize()` read it as a different title from the recorded `O(n²)`. The `²` was dropped outright, while `^2` kept its digit behind a separator. Accented letters were also dropped outright. `normalize()` now folds spelling before comparing: it unwraps TeX, applies Unicode NFKD and drops combining marks, names Greek letters (`µ` → `μ` → `mu`, meeting `\mu`), and compares with every separator removed.

**The order of the TeX passes matters.**
1. Formatting commands (`\textbf`, `\mathcal`, …) go first and keep their argument.
2. Letter accents (`\v{c}`) go next. They count as accents only when followed by `{`, so `\cite` and `\boldsymbol` aren't eaten.
3. Then symbol accents and escaped punctuation (`\"o`, `\&`).
4. Only then do remaining control words become their names.

`\varepsilon`, `ε` and `ϵ` all reach `epsilon`, since the variant glyph is the same letter.

**What it must not fold** is pinned in tests: `\mu` vs `\nu`, `n^2` vs `n^3`, and the AdamW nickname. The accepted cost is that `data set` equals `dataset`. For "is this the same paper" that is wanted.

**Not checked on the real case.** `LIT-655` lives in anthology-of-the-sota, which this session can't reach. The issue's own acceptance step covers it: after release, its `source-ok:` should be reported as excusing nothing. No `source-ok:` in this repository or its examples flips.

## Unrevisited summaries: a check that only speaks before the commit

*2026-10-02 20:07:13*

**[#326](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/326).** The check compares the working tree against HEAD ([ADR-tmp4osmu](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-tmp4osmu.md)). That makes it a pre-commit check: it is silent in CI and after the commit. That is the moment the issue argued for, and the shallow checkouts rule out walking history anyway.

**The acknowledgement is what needed design.** Every other `-ok:` directive is reported stale once it excuses nothing. Here, though, the check goes blind at the commit, so a correct `summary-ok:` would have been called stale on the very next lint. Two fixes went in together:
- The directive names the version it answers (`summary-ok: v7`), so it cannot silently cover later bumps.
- Staleness is judged only while a bump is uncommitted. A test pins the case the first draft got wrong: an amendment committed with its acknowledgement, followed by an unrelated typo fix. That typo fix made the directive look stale.

**Cost:** one `git diff --name-only HEAD` per lint, plus one `git show` per changed document whose version moved. Unchanged documents cost nothing.

**Fired once on a real case:** [ADR-001](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-001.md) bumped to v3 in the working tree with its summary untouched. It was reported at the `summary:` line, then reverted.
